REPORT
1          The Department of Heavy Industry is concerned with the development of the Heavy Engineering Industries, Machine Tool Industries, Heavy Electrical Industries, Industrial Machineries and Auto-Industries. The Industries covered by this Department provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy, including power, rail and road transport. They also cater to the requirements of equipment for basic industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, fertilizers, refineries, petrochemicals, shipping, textiles, paper, cement, sugar etc. The Department is responsible for the development of a wide range of intermediate engineering products like castings, forgings, diesel engines, industrial gears and gearboxes. It is also vested with the administrative charge of 49 Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs).
1.1       The PSEs under the administrative control of the Department are engaged in the manufacturing of Engineering/Capital Goods, Consultancy and Contracting Activities. The total investment (Gross Block) in 49 Public Sector Enterprises under the Department of Heavy Industry was about Rs.8052.00 Crores till 31ST March, 2001 employing about 1,46,558 lakh persons.
1.2       The Department holds interactions with various Industry Councils and evolves Plans for their growth. The Department also assists Public Sector Enterprises through policy initiatives, resolution of problems relating to tariffs and trade, technological collaboration, up- gradation and Research & Development, etc.

2.5       The Committee noted that many of the Central PSEs are making losses due to their inability to their face the competition, obsolete R&D, high cost of production, shortage of work orders, etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry should infuse capital, state of the art technology and entrepreneurship into  potentially viable PSEs so as the make these `Modern Temples' capable to face the private sector MNCs in the  consumer economy.2.6       In the wake of growing financial   crunch in many of the Central PSEs, the Committee recommends that the Government should provide financial assistance in the form of working capital, Non-Plan loan, Government guarantee, etc.  to  PSEs which are potentially viable.
2.7     In order to overcome the constraints of the Central PSEs, concerted efforts have been made including restructuring of various Heavy Industry PSEs. The BIFR has sanctioned revival plans   in the case of 12 PSEs, which are under implementation.  On its own Government has approved restructuring in seven other cases. Action has been initiated for converting 28 PSEs into Joint Ventures/disinvestment. As a last resort, seven unviable PSEs have been closed. Unviable units of some of the   PSEs have also been        closed. Government has approved reservation of orders for Hindustan Cable Ltd. from DOT/MTNL and from BSNL for Instrumentation Ltd. Ministry of Railways   has been     persuaded to place orders for wagons on the wagon building PSEs of the Department of Heavy Industry.
2.8       The Department also stated that a White Paper defining the future of the PSEs under the Department of Heavy Industry based on the Public Sector Policy of the Government is under preparation.  The Department informed the Committee that Public Sector Policy of the Government has focused on the following areas: -
·
        Restructure and revive potentially viable PSEs;
·        Bring down Govt. equity in all non-strategic PSEs to 26% or lower, if necessary;
·        Fully protect the interests of workers; and
·        Close down PSEs, which cannot be revived.
 
2.9       The Committee recommends that while rationalising the Government   equity in non-strategic PSEs, interests of the workers should be protected fully.

RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT OF AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY      
4          The Department stated that R&D and technology development is the backbone of the Automotive Industry. Because of this fact, a cess had been imposed on Automobiles with effect from 1st January 1984 and on tractors from 1st October 1985 at the rate of 18% advalorem to finance R&D in the industry. The cess is being collected by the Department of Revenue and forms part of the Consolidated Fund of India. The Ministry of Finance is allocating a portion of this fund through the Budget to the DHI under the Head of Account ‘Cess’ for the Development Council for Automobile and Allied Industries.
4.1       It was stated by the Department that with the fragmented automobile industry in India, it is not feasible for the individual units to establish full-fledged R&D set up and testing facilitates. Hence there is a need to establish R&D testing facilities, which will cater to the industry as a whole. With the introduction of new and stricter emission norms as well as safety standards, more & more R&D facilities are needed in the country to meet the demand of the Industry.   The Department further added that the Development Council for Automotive and Allied Industry (DCAAI) allocates Cess funds for research and development to establish R&D institutions through a Cess Committee chaired by Secretary, Department of Heavy Industry. 
4.2       The Department has informed the Committee that with progressive introduction of new and stricter emission norms as well as safety standards, more and more testing facilities are needed in the country to meet the demand of  Industry. There is also a need to look at other areas of product and process related research with a view to propelling India’s Automotive Industry into a higher league and for surviving the import surge under WTO regime. The plan-budget will be used to these areas of concern.
4.3       The Department also informed the Committee that the Government has adopted the following Policies to encourage the testing facilities for Auto Sector:
·        Budget enhanced from Rs.8.00 crores in 2001-02 to Rs.25 crores in 2002-03
·        Facilities to be provided at 6 or 7 different Centres in the country at a total cost of Rs.700.00 crores to meet regulations relating to safety and emission norms.
·        Plan component during the 10th Five Year Plan is Rs.350.00 crores and balance will be met from the non-plan from cess fund.
4.4       The Department further added that at present the cess is levied @ 1/8% i.e. 0.125% over and above the excise duty.   In difference to the recommendations made by the Committee last year, Department of Heavy Industry has already taken up the matter with the Ministry of Finance for (i) enhancement in the rate of levy of cess from 0.05% to 0.25% and (ii) for increasing the allocation of collected cess to that Department. While the Finance Ministry has enhanced the allocation of cess from the existing level of Rs.10.00 crores to Rs.25.00 crores in the Budget Estimates for the financial year 2002-03, the rate of cess has not been revised.
4.5       The Committee has noted that the cess to improve R&D in Automotive   Industry has been increased from Rs.10.00 crores to Rs.25.00 crores in the budget estimates of 2002-03.  However, the rate of cess has not been revised from 0.05% to 0.25% over   and above the excise   duty    as earnestly demanded by the automotive sector.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the DHI should, at the first instance, take up this matter with the Ministry of Finance and resolve to save the automotive industry.
4.6       The Department further stated that there is an urgent need to ensure higher commitment on research and development activities by the industry in the emerging circumstances. At present industry is spending only about 0.2% of their sales turnover on research and development. In most developed countries the spending on R&D in automobile sector ranges between 3% to 4%.  Realising this fact the Government has provided for special incentives to research and development activities in the Auto Policy, which has been announced recently.
4.7       The Committee is constrained to note that the Indian Automotive Industry is spending only 0.2% of their sales   turnover on R&D as against 3% to 4% spent by most auto industries in the developed Countries.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the DHI should create a separate corpus of funds to meet the emerging requirements of R&D of the auto industries.
4.8       It was informed by the Department that the cess funds have been used to create necessary infrastructure for the automotive sector. The infrastructure created includes facilities for testing of vehicle for the purpose of assessing their conformity to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules. The objectives of the Cess funded projects range from testing vehicles for roadworthiness, to testing of components and sub-assemblies from the angle of safety and environmental protection. Keeping in view these objectives, cess funds have been utilized over the years to strengthen the capability of the research institutes in Automotive Sector-particularly Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI), Pune; Vehicle Research Development Establishment (VRDE), Ahmednagar and Central Institute of Road Transport (CIRT), Pune, which undertake testing of new vehicles for their homologation i.e. testing of various components and vehicle parameters to check compliance with Central Motor Vehicle Rules (CMVR) requirements and road worthiness. This Department is working on National Testing facility in consultation with concerned agencies like Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM) etc. to meet the emerging requirements.4.9       The Department informed the Committee that DHI has taken the following efforts to enhance the R&D facilities:
Ø
                  A National Project on `coal gasification’ for power generation has been included in Budget 2002-03. Development of this technology will result in: -
·        Better utilisation of high ash content Indian coal.
·        Improvement in efficiency.
·        Reduction in pollution levels.
4.10     The Committee notes that cess funds have been   utilised over the years to strengthen the infrastructure of the research institutes of ARAI, VRDE, CIRT, etc.  for testing of various   auto components to meeting regulations relating to safety and emission norms.  The Committee recommends   that Department of  Heavy Industry should analyse the results achieved by these Institutes in the field of testing new vehicles for their homologations from the safety and environment point of view and take appropriate measures.
4.11     It may be pointed out that Electric Vehicles (E.V.s) are making their  own contribution towards making our environment free from pollution. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Excise Duty on 3-wheeler Electric Vehicles may be reduced from existing 16% to 1 %. The Committee also recommends that the Basic Customs Duty on components of the Electric Vehicle may be reduced from the existing 15- 35% to 5%.
4.12     In the Auto Policy, compatible with WTO guidelines, which were announced by the Government on 7th March 2002 it has been indicated that as an impetus for the development of electric vehicles, an appropriate long term fiscal structure shall be put in place to facilitate their acceptance vis-à-vis vehicles based on conventional fuels. Already Scooters India Limited, a Public Sector Enterprises, is running a pilot project with financial assistance from the Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources for establishing commercial viability of the battery run three wheeler vehicles.
4.13     The objectives of the Auto Policy as announced by the Department of Heavy Industry on 7th March, 2002 are as under: -
·        Promoting a globally competitive Auto Industry and developing India as a major source of World class auto components.
·        100% Foreign Direct Investment without any minimum capitalisation norms now permitted in this Sector.
·        other significant objectives of the Policy are higher value addition through appropriate fiscal measures, promotion of low emission fuel technologies, alternative fuels and hybrid vehicles.

ii         The basic customs duty on newsprint imports continues to be pegged at 5% as against the WTO-bound rate of 25%, indiscriminate dumping of newsprint is taking place.  Ironically, newsprint also does not attract Special Additional Duty (SAD) while domestic newsprint manufacturers have to pay local sales tax, entry tax, etc.  The ‘Disguised Imports’ of writing and printing paper and ‘stock lots’ are still vitiating the domestic paper market and posing difficulties for domestic paper manufacturers, eroding their capability to become globally competitive.  Import duty on newsprint should, therefore, be enhanced to the WTO-bound rate of 25%.  Imports should also be regulated as per the genuine requirements of the newspaper publishers by insisting on a third party certificate from any independent international quality surveyor (not the manufacturer of newsprint).  Newsprint import also should attract SAD as applicable to other products.
iii        The Government of India has treated the Light Weight Coated (LWC) paper as a variety of newsprint since June 1998 for customs duty purposes attracting only 5 % duty.  In the guise of LWC, a lot of coated and uncoated papers are being imported into the country disturbing the market equilibrium.  Even though production capacity exists, domestic manufacturers do not find it worthwhile to produce LWC on account of the non-existence of a level-playing field.  LWC should be classified as paper and not be clubbed with Newsprint.  Import of LWC should attract SAD and Counter Vailing Duty (CVD), as domestic production of equivalent varieties attracts local taxes and basic excise duty (currently 16%).
iv       Excise Notifications issued by the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance including Notification No. 8/2002-CE and 9/2002-CE both dated 1st March, 2002 allowing continuance of payment of zero excise duty by a section of paper industry up to the first clearance of aggregate quantity not exceeding 3500 tpa of paper of Unconventional Raw Material (UCRM) are causing substantial losses to the Exchequer (estimated to be about Rs.500 crores) as a large number of paper mills are avoiding the payment of excise duty (misusing the said dispensation) and thereby vitiating the market characteristics.  When the imperative is to consolidate and create world-scale (and world-class) capacities, this lop-sided exemption dispensation has acted as a dampener for capacity expansion and technology up gradation, besides breeding unhealthy practices in the market place.

PREFERENCE FOR DOMESTICALLY MANUFACTURED GOODS
 
1.         The Borrower may, with the agreement of the Bank, grant a margin of preference in the evaluation of bids under ICB procedures to bids offering certain goods manufactured in the country of the Borrower, when compared to bids offering such goods manufactured elsewhere. In such cases, bidding documents shall clearly indicate any preference to be granted to domestic manufactured goods and the information required to establish the eligibility of a bid for such preference. The nationality of the manufacturer or supplier is not a condition for such eligibility. The methods and stages set forth hereunder shall be followed in the evaluation and comparison of bids.2.         For comparison, responsive bids shall be classified in one of the following three groups:
a.
       Group A: bids offering goods manufactured in the country of the Borrower if the bidder establishes to the satisfaction of the Borrower and the Bank that (i) labor, raw material and components from within the country of the Borrower will account for more than 30 percent of the EXW price of the product offered, and (ii) the production facility in which those goods will be manufactured or assembled has been engaged in manufacturing/assembling such goods at least since the time of bid submission.
b.      Group B: all other bids offering goods from within the country of the Borrower.
c.       Group C: bids offering the goods from abroad and to be directly imported.
3.         The EXW price quoted by a Group A bidder shall include all duties and taxes paid or payable on the basic materials or components purchased in the domestic market or imported. Similarly, prices quoted by Group B bidders shall include all duties and taxes on components and raw materials. The price quoted by Group A and B bidders shall exclude the sales and similar taxes on the finished product. The price quoted by Group C bidders shall be on CIF or CIP border point or other destination, exclusive of customs duties and other import taxes.
4.         In the first step, all evaluated bids in each group shall be compared to determine the lowest evaluated bid in each. Such lowest evaluated bids shall then be compared with each other and if, as a result of this comparison, a bid from Group A or Group B is the lowest, it shall be selected for the award.
5.         If, as a result of the comparison under paragraph 4 above, the lowest evaluated bid is a bid from Group C, all Group C bids shall be further compared with the lowest evaluated bid from Group A after adding to the evaluated bid price of the imported goods offered in each Group C bid, for the purpose of this further comparison only, an amount equal to: (i) the amount of duties and other related import charges which a nonexempt importer would have to pay for the importation of the goods offered in such Group C bid; or (ii) 15 percent of the CIF or CIP bid price of such goods if said duties and charges exceed 15 percent of such price. If the Group A bid in such further comparison is the lowest, it shall be selected for the award; if not, the lowest evaluated bid from Group C, as determined from the comparison under paragraph 4, shall be selected.

5.         The Committee then adjourned  for lunch  and re-assembled  at 3.00 p.m. to resume the discussions with the representatives of    BHEL, HPC, HMT, REIL, HCL and BYNL.
 
6.         Resuming in the post lunch session the Chairman welcomed the representatives of BHEL, HPC, HMT, REIL, HCL and BYNL and asked them to express their views on the provisions of the budget affecting their respective company. 
6.1       Shri K.G. Ramachandran, CMD, BHEL, viewed that budget since last two years had not been  announcing  industry  specific solutions.  He  informed  that  increase of surcharge by  3 per cent  on  direct  tax front would have negative impact on  BHEL of about Rs. 7.8 crores  while the
withdrawal of 10 per cent dividend tax would put  BHEL on the receiving end.  The reduction of excise duty on item like copper, tin etc. (used by BHEL) would have a positive impact of Rs. 2.5 crores.  The outlay in the APDRP, i.e. Accelerated Power Development and Rural Programme, have been increased  to Rs. 3,500 crores from 1500 crores.  The Schemes like the Fund Distribution Schemes and modernization of existing power schemes would be beneficial to BHEL since it would enable it to get orders for modernization of Power plants.
 
6.2       Shri Raji Philip, CMD HPC was of the view that the budget was very disappointing for the paper industry because as far as writing and printing paper industry was concerned , the duty reduction from 35 to 30 as against the  WTO bound rate of 40 per cent was going to affect the paper industry adversely.  He desired the rationalisation of custom duty in general and referred the imposition of industry tax on news print by Tamil Nadu Government and maintained that budget was not giving us any comfort signals for the newsprint and writing , paper industry. He  further suggested to change the raw material pattern  i.e. use of recycled fibre instead of using virgin fibre (wood). 
6.3       Shri S.C. Gupta, CMD, BYNL furnished the details of financial performance of the company, rationalisation of manpower through VRS grant, purchase -preference and status of work order, and revival package which is under the consideration of the Government. 
 
6.4       Shri H.S. Sanga, Executive Director of HMT stated that country's tractor manufacturing is to the tune of  4.75 lakhs but its demand is 2 lakhs only and this gap is due to lack of mechanisation of agriculture and therefore he suggested  that NABARD be given sufficient grant for lending liberal loans to the farmers.  He further pointed out to  the smuggling of modules which adversely affect the cost competitiveness of watch wing of HMT.  He further answered the questions raised by the Members pertaining to the market research and quality maintenance, mechanism to enhance the purchasing capacity of farmers, measures to boost export of tractors position of printing machinery ,VRS in HMT in general and Nanital factory in particular and progress made in regard to the disinvestment of  various wings of HMT.
 6.5       Speaking on behalf of Rajasthan Electronics Instrumentation Ltd. Shri M.M. Bhardwaj, MD, was of the view that the proposal of the Government in the budget to reduce the duty on a product namely, solar photovoltaic module system, from 100 per cent to 60 % would have a major impact on the market therefore the same should be retained at 100%. .  He further that if excise duty imposed on electronic milk tester ( used for checking fat contents) is waived the product might be popularized even to the village strata.  He further gave the details of the balance sheet of the company  alongwith diversification programmes and other future planning, R&D  activities and status of technology in  the company.
